note.question: What determines reassigning sites to teams to maximize effectiveness?
note.overview: United Nations Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) 3.8 states that health coverage should be universal by 2030. This is challenging in rural and poor areas. To address this challenge, mobile outreach teams of healthcare workers visit a fixed set of remote sites to provide healthcare services.

source.quote: To address this challenge, mobile outreach teams of healthcare workers visit a fixed set of remote sites to provide healthcare services.
Solving this problem through a central planner does not fit the context: outreach teams commonly have a high degree of decision-making autonomy.
Managerial implications: Humanitarian organizations currently deploy mobile outreach teams to provide a wide variety of health services.
We present several useful insights for decision makers in humanitarian organizations when making design choices, taking account of context.
A later start time can lead to a more crowded sched­ ule, which can cause long wait times and subsequently client dropouts.
Each team has a given capacity, that is, the maximum number of visits it can undertake in the planning period, denoted by ct.

source.section: Decentralized Decision Rules for Site Reassign
source.quote: The algorithm is as follows: (1) set all visit frequencies to f LB (the lowest feasible frequency in the set F) for each site; (2) greedily pick the site with the highest ˆµst and set the visit frequency to the highest feasible frequency in the set F given the team’s remaining capacity; (3) repeat step 2 until the team’s capacity has been allo­ cated.
